**Alliant University** is a [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university")[for-profit university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For-profit_higher_education_in_the_United_States "For-profit higher education in the United States")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-EdDive2015-1) with its main campus in [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego"), five additional campuses in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") ([San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irvine,_California "Irvine, California"), [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento"), and [Fresno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresno,_California "Fresno, California")) and one campus in [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"). Its enrollment is approximately 4,000 students, of whom 95% are graduate students.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alliant_University&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Alliant was formed in 2001 by the combination of two older institutions: the [California School of Professional Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_School_of_Professional_Psychology "California School of Professional Psychology") (CSPP) and [United States International University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_International_University "United States International University") (USIU).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:11-2) Like the institutions that it descended from, Alliant has its home campus in San Diego, California. Until 2007, USIU also had a Europe campus in a former public school in the UK, which was used as a site for many films, including the _Harry Potter_ series.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-3)

USIU is the descendant of the original **Balboa School of Law** founded by Leland Ghent Stanford as a private graduate institution in 1924. The name was changed to **Balboa University** and then, in 1952, to **California Western University**. With the name change to California Western University the school relocated to an oceanside campus in [Point Loma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Loma,_San_Diego "Point Loma, San Diego") (the site of present-day [Point Loma Nazarene University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Loma_Nazarene_University "Point Loma Nazarene University")). In 1968, the school's name was changed to [United States International University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_International_University "United States International University") with the vision to become a global university. Land was purchased for a new campus in [Scripps Ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scripps_Ranch,_San_Diego "Scripps Ranch, San Diego"), and all USIU operations were moved there by 1973.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-Ross-4) The law school, however, retained the name of [California Western School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Western_School_of_Law "California Western School of Law") and moved to a new downtown location. In 1975 it split off to become an independent institution that is still in operation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-Ross-4)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Alliant_SD_entrance.jpg/250px-Alliant_SD_entrance.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alliant_SD_entrance.jpg)

The entrance to the San Diego campus

William C. Rust was the president of California Western University who ushered in the transformation to USIU and led the school for the next 37 years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:5-6) Rust's vision was "to create global understanding through a single university with campuses all over the world.".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:6-7) The founding goal for USIU was a focus on "human excellence" over "intellectual excellence."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:6-7) By 1971, Rust had transformed the former small liberal arts school of California Western University into what the _[San Diego Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San\_Diego\_Reader "San Diego Reader")_ referred to as an "international phenomenon."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:6-7) Besides the main Scripps Ranch campus, USIU had developed a network of campuses both nationally in [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui"), [Steamboat Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat_Springs,_Colorado "Steamboat Springs, Colorado"), and [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam") as well as internationally, with branch campuses in: [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"), [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") and [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:7-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-11) In 1986, Rust was still breaking new ground for buildings and maintaining a focus on further expansion in Latin America, the Middle East, Europe, and Russia.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:5-6) But by 1990, after 37 years of leading the university and enduring several rocky financial episodes, Rust was removed of all governing power by the board of trustees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:5-6)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:7-9) Gary Hays, former chancellor of the Minnesota State University, took over as president of USIU in April 1990 and reorganized the University into just two remaining colleges; arts and sciences and business administration.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-12) In 1999, the [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") campus became its own independent entity known as [United States International University Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_International_University_Africa "United States International University Africa").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-13)

In 2001 the California School of Professional Psychology and United States International University merged to become **Alliant International University**, taking over the Scripps Ranch campus of USIU. At first Alliant was a nonprofit university like its predecessors. In February 2015, Alliant became a for-profit [benefit corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benefit_corporation "Benefit corporation") and part of the Arist Education System, a subsidiary of [Bertelsmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann "Bertelsmann").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-14)

In January 2026, Alliant International University rebranded as Alliant University to reflect the institution’s transition to a primarily U.S.-based university.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-15)

## Schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alliant_University&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Schools")]

Alliant University is composed of several academic schools:

*   [California School of Professional Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_School_of_Professional_Psychology "California School of Professional Psychology")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:0-16) The California School of Professional Psychology (CSPP) was founded in 1969 under the auspices of the California Psychological Association. CSPP offers programs in clinical psychology, clinical counseling, and marital and family therapy.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:0-16)
*   California School of Management & Leadership[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:1-17) In 2011, Alliant International University renamed their management school to Alliant School of Management then to California School of Management & Leadership in 2018. Formerly the [Marshall Goldsmith School of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Goldsmith_School_of_Management "Marshall Goldsmith School of Management"), named for organizational consultant and executive coach [Marshall Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Goldsmith "Marshall Goldsmith"), the School of Management offers a 4-year BSBA program, master's and doctoral degrees in Business, Management, and Leadership.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:1-17)
*   California School of Education[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:2-18) The California School of Education offers programs in teaching, school psychology, educational leadership, and [teaching English to speakers of other languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_as_a_second_or_foreign_language "English as a second or foreign language").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:2-18)
*   California School of Forensic Studies[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:3-19) The California School of Forensic Studies offers programs in criminology and criminal justice.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:3-19)

## Accreditation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alliant_University&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Accreditation")]

Alliant, including all of its programs, is [accredited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_accreditation_in_the_United_States "Higher education accreditation in the United States") by the [WASC Senior College and University Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WASC_Senior_College_and_University_Commission "WASC Senior College and University Commission").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-22)

*   The university's education programs are approved by the [California State Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Board_of_Education "California State Board of Education").
*   Alliant's teach credentialing programs are approved by the [California Commission on Teacher Credentialing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCTC "CCTC").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-23)
*   [Clinical psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_psychology "Clinical psychology") programs are accredited by the [American Psychological Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Psychological_Association "American Psychological Association") (APA).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-24)
*   Alliant's marital and family therapy programs are accredited by the Commission on Accreditation for Marriage and Family Therapy Education.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-25)
*   Alliant's clinical counseling program is accredited by Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs (CACREP) cacrep.org[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-26)
*   The Bachelor and Master of Science in Nursing programs at Alliant are accredited by the Commission on Collegiate Nursing Education (CCNE).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-27)
*   The Master of Social Work program at Alliant is accredited by the Council on Social Work Education (CSWE).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-28)
*   Alliant’s entry-level occupational therapy master’s degree program has applied for accreditation and has been granted Candidacy Status by the Accreditation Council for Occupational Therapy Education (ACOTE) of the American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-29)

## Recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alliant_University&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

Alliant was included in _GI Jobs_ magazine's 2013 list of Military-Friendly Schools, the third year in a row the university had been included in this listing. It was also included on the _Military Times EDGE_ magazine's list of Best for Vets Colleges in 2010 and 2011; in 2011, Alliant was ranked #10 on the list, making it the highest-ranked non-traditional university in California.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-33)

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alliant_University&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [United States International University §Division I sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_International_University#Division_I_sports "United States International University")

During the 1980s and 1990s, prior to its merger with Alliant, the USIU Gulls fielded several Division I teams. The football team produced [six professional football players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:United_States_International_Gulls_football_players "Category:United States International Gulls football players")[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-34) and was once briefly coached by the legendary player and coach [Sid Gillman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Gillman "Sid Gillman").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:8-35) USIU's international student body allowed it to field a competitive [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") hockey team, the [USIU Gulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_International_Gulls_men's_ice_hockey "United States International Gulls men's ice hockey"), which was the only [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA "NCAA") team "west of the Rockies."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:9-36) However, in 1990 after 10 successful years and producing two [NHL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hockey_League "National Hockey League") players, the program was dropped due to the rising cost of traveling to distant campuses to compete.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-37) USIU also maintained an [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") basketball team.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-:10-38) USIU's women's softball team appeared in one [Women's College World Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_College_World_Series "Women's College World Series") in [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_AIAW_Women's_College_World_Series "1982 AIAW Women's College World Series").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-Plummer-39)

Alliant University maintained a sports program for a few years but phased out its intercollegiate athletics programs in 2007.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliant_University#cite_note-40)

# College Names at UNI, 1968--

‌Prior to 1967, when the school gained university status, there was no collegiate structure between the instructional departments and the school's upper administration.In the early days of the school, instructional department heads reported to the President.After President Latham took office in 1928, he instituted substantial administrative re-organization, appointed a Dean of the Faculty, and helped to develop faculty governance.But departments maintained a fairly independent status.Some departments, such as Education, English, Science, and Social Science, were very large. Other departments functioned with quite small faculties.

But university status brought with it the need for a collegiate administrative structure.Groups of departments with similar curricula needed to be organized into colleges governed by a College Dean.Some departments fell into place easily; other departments required a stretching of collegiate boundaries and definitions in order to find a home.

In 1968 the university organized four colleges: Business and Behavioral Sciences, Education, Humanities and Fine Arts, and Natural Science.The Graduate College was somewhat different from the undergraduate colleges in that it would be constituted of a graduate faculty rather than individual departments; the Graduate College was noted in the 1968-1969 UNI budget as having "No formal budget set up by May Board (of Regents) meeting; may establish later in the year by transfer from unallocated funds."The undergraduate colleges were set up with budget lines for Deans and office staffs. The College of Business and Behavioral Sciences included four departments, the Business and Business Education Department, the Home Economics Department, the Psychology Department, and the still undifferentiated Social Science Department. The College of Education included five instructional departments: the still undifferentiated Education and Educational Psychology Department, the Library Science Department, the Physical Education for Men Department, the Physical Education for Women Department, and the Teaching Department.The College of Humanities and Fine Arts included: Art, English Language and Literature, Foreign Languages, Music, and Speech. The College of Natural Sciences included: Biology, Chemistry, Industrial Arts and Technology, and Physics and Earth Science.

In 1969, the old all-encompassing Social Science Department in the College of Business and Behavioral Sciences was differentiated into five departments: Economics, Geography, History, Political Science, and Sociology and Anthropology. Also in that year, the Philosophy and Religion Department emerged from the English Language and Literature Department, and the Graduate College was formally organized and budgeted.

In 1970 the Physics and Earth Science Department split into the Physics Department and the Earth Science Department. In 1971 the Education and Educational Psychology Department split into three departments: Curriculum and Instruction, Educational Psychology and Foundations, and School Administration and Personnel Services. With that, the university had completed its initial round of department differentiation.

Over the years since then, several new departments have been established or phased out, and quite a few have split or changed names to reflect a shifted focus or more contemporary terminology. These [instructional department name changes](https://scua.library.uni.edu/library_scua/university-archives/articles/instructional-department-names-1876-alphabetical-list) are treated elsewhere. However, only one of the original colleges has changed its name and only one new college has been established since the initial collegiate organization in the late 1960s. These two significant changes are linked.

Enrollment and interest in the study of business surged in the late 1970s and 1980s. In 1969 the Business and Business Education Department had split into the Business Department and the Business Education and Office Administration Department. In 1981 the Business Department emerged from the College of Business and Behavioral Sciences as the School of Business, with collegiate status and its own array of differentiated business-related departments. The College of Business and Behavioral Sciences then became the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences. And in the only instance of a department moving from one college to another, the Economics Department left the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences to join the School of Business in 1985.

In 1989, the School of Business became the College of Business Administration.

Please note that this information is not always regularly updated, may contain inaccuracies,and may not be comprehensive. # College Names at UNI, 1968--

‌Prior to 1967, when the school gained university status, there was no collegiate structure between the instructional departments and the school's upper administration.In the early days of the school, instructional department heads reported to the President.After President Latham took office in 1928, he instituted substantial administrative re-organization, appointed a Dean of the Faculty, and helped to develop faculty governance.But departments maintained a fairly independent status.Some departments, such as Education, English, Science, and Social Science, were very large. Other departments functioned with quite small faculties.

But university status brought with it the need for a collegiate administrative structure.Groups of departments with similar curricula needed to be organized into colleges governed by a College Dean.Some departments fell into place easily; other departments required a stretching of collegiate boundaries and definitions in order to find a home.

In 1968 the university organized four colleges: Business and Behavioral Sciences, Education, Humanities and Fine Arts, and Natural Science.The Graduate College was somewhat different from the undergraduate colleges in that it would be constituted of a graduate faculty rather than individual departments; the Graduate College was noted in the 1968-1969 UNI budget as having "No formal budget set up by May Board (of Regents) meeting; may establish later in the year by transfer from unallocated funds."The undergraduate colleges were set up with budget lines for Deans and office staffs. The College of Business and Behavioral Sciences included four departments, the Business and Business Education Department, the Home Economics Department, the Psychology Department, and the still undifferentiated Social Science Department. The College of Education included five instructional departments: the still undifferentiated Education and Educational Psychology Department, the Library Science Department, the Physical Education for Men Department, the Physical Education for Women Department, and the Teaching Department.The College of Humanities and Fine Arts included: Art, English Language and Literature, Foreign Languages, Music, and Speech. The College of Natural Sciences included: Biology, Chemistry, Industrial Arts and Technology, and Physics and Earth Science.

In 1969, the old all-encompassing Social Science Department in the College of Business and Behavioral Sciences was differentiated into five departments: Economics, Geography, History, Political Science, and Sociology and Anthropology. Also in that year, the Philosophy and Religion Department emerged from the English Language and Literature Department, and the Graduate College was formally organized and budgeted.

In 1970 the Physics and Earth Science Department split into the Physics Department and the Earth Science Department. In 1971 the Education and Educational Psychology Department split into three departments: Curriculum and Instruction, Educational Psychology and Foundations, and School Administration and Personnel Services. With that, the university had completed its initial round of department differentiation.

Over the years since then, several new departments have been established or phased out, and quite a few have split or changed names to reflect a shifted focus or more contemporary terminology. These [instructional department name changes](https://scua.library.uni.edu/library_scua/university-archives/articles/instructional-department-names-1876-alphabetical-list) are treated elsewhere. However, only one of the original colleges has changed its name and only one new college has been established since the initial collegiate organization in the late 1960s. These two significant changes are linked.

Enrollment and interest in the study of business surged in the late 1970s and 1980s. In 1969 the Business and Business Education Department had split into the Business Department and the Business Education and Office Administration Department. In 1981 the Business Department emerged from the College of Business and Behavioral Sciences as the School of Business, with collegiate status and its own array of differentiated business-related departments. The College of Business and Behavioral Sciences then became the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences. And in the only instance of a department moving from one college to another, the Economics Department left the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences to join the School of Business in 1985.

In 1989, the School of Business became the College of Business Administration.

about it.— Per Austrin, Bruce Mer ry, and Jakub Onufry Wojtaszczyk

Summary

The contest started out with the University of Warsaw making an amazing start, at one point being in the lead with 5 problems solved while the team in second place still only had 2 prob-lems solved. But after solvi ng seven proble ms in the ﬁrst two hours, they slowed down, and ultimately ended up with 8 solved in 4th place.The last hour of the contest was very exciting in the judge’s room (and for careful viewers of ICPC Live as well), with MIT and Moscow State battling for the ﬁrst place: 3 minutes into the last hour, MIT took the lead by solving K in the ﬁrst attempt, but a few minutes later Moscow State solved both I and K in quick succession, putting them ahead by one problem.However their penalty time was pretty high due to several incorrect attempts on K, so MIT had a window of 30 minutes to solve another problem and take the lead. With just 30 seconds remaining of that window, they submitted a correct submission on I and regained ﬁrst place,with the same number of problems solved and a single penalty minute less than Moscow.Howev er, their lead was short-liv ed: just a minute later, 21 minutes before the end of the contest, Moscow submitted a correct solution on F, reaching 10 solved problems, which earned them the victory.

Congratulations to Moscow State University

for successfully defending their title as the ICPC World Champions!

Problem C: Checks Post Facto

Solved by 0 teams.Shortest judge solution: 3955 bytes.

0 6 0 1 2 0 1 8 0 2 4 0 3 0 0 1 0 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 A C W A T L E R T E

While the judges ﬁgured this for the third hardest problem, it turned out to be the hardest,and only unsolved, problem. The probl em is mostly a tricky implem entati on problem. W e can start construc ting a soluti on iterative ly: start with an empty boar d, and play throug h the moves until an inconsistency is found; then go back and add/modify a piece until everything works out, according to the following conditions:

•

If there is no piece where a piece is meant to move from, add a man.

•

If a man moves backwards without having been promoted, replace it (at the start) with a king.

•

If a piece captures but there is nothing to jump over, add a man there (of appropriate color).These conditions used the following key observation: there is never any beneﬁt to placing a king when a man would sufﬁce, since a king might only force more choices later.After the above has converged, there is still the problem of forced captures. If at some point a player does not take a forced capture, there must be another piece blocking it. It might as well be a man, but the color is unknown. At this point one can just try both options (recursively),and stop once one has found a solution that doesn’t require more blocking pieces and does not contain a contradiction. While there are 32 spaces on the board, in practice this completes very quickly as it is difﬁcult to set up situations where large numbers of choices need to be made correctly.

Solution sketches

Disclaimer

This is an unofﬁci al analysi s of some possible ways to solve the pr oblem s of the ACM ICPC World Finals 2019. They are not intended to give a complete solution, but rather to outline some appr oach that can be used to solve the problem. If some of the termino logy or algorith ms mentione d below are not familiar to you, your favorite search engine should be able to help. If you ﬁnd an error,please send an e-mail to

austrin@kth.se

about it.— Per Austrin, Bruce Mer ry, and Jakub Onufry Wojtaszczyk

Summary

The contest started out with the University of Warsaw making an amazing start, at one point being in the lead with 5 problems solved while the team in second place still only had 2 prob-lems solved. But after solvi ng seven proble ms in the ﬁrst two hours, they slowed down, and ultimately ended up with 8 solved in 4th place.The last hour of the contest was very exciting in the judge’s room (and for careful viewers of ICPC Live as well), with MIT and Moscow State battling for the ﬁrst place: 3 minutes into the last hour, MIT took the lead by solving K in the ﬁrst attempt, but a few minutes later Moscow State solved both I and K in quick succession, putting them ahead by one problem.However their penalty time was pretty high due to several incorrect attempts on K, so MIT had a window of 30 minutes to solve another problem and take the lead. With just 30 seconds remaining of that window, they submitted a correct submission on I and regained ﬁrst place,with the same number of problems solved and a single penalty minute less than Moscow.Howev er, their lead was short-liv ed: just a minute later, 21 minutes before the end of the contest, Moscow submitted a correct solution on F, reaching 10 solved problems, which earned them the victory.

Congratulations to Moscow State University

for successfully defending their title as the ICPC World Champions!

Problem C: Checks Post Facto

Solved by 0 teams.Shortest judge solution: 3955 bytes.

0 6 0 1 2 0 1 8 0 2 4 0 3 0 0 1 0 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 A C W A T L E R T E

While the judges ﬁgured this for the third hardest problem, it turned out to be the hardest,and only unsolved, problem. The probl em is mostly a tricky implem entati on problem. W e can start construc ting a soluti on iterative ly: start with an empty boar d, and play throug h the moves until an inconsistency is found; then go back and add/modify a piece until everything works out, according to the following conditions:

•

If there is no piece where a piece is meant to move from, add a man.

•

If a man moves backwards without having been promoted, replace it (at the start) with a king.

•

If a piece captures but there is nothing to jump over, add a man there (of appropriate color).These conditions used the following key observation: there is never any beneﬁt to placing a king when a man would sufﬁce, since a king might only force more choices later.After the above has converged, there is still the problem of forced captures. If at some point a player does not take a forced capture, there must be another piece blocking it. It might as well be a man, but the color is unknown. At this point one can just try both options (recursively),and stop once one has found a solution that doesn’t require more blocking pieces and does not contain a contradiction. While there are 32 spaces on the board, in practice this completes very quickly as it is difﬁcult to set up situations where large numbers of choices need to be made correctly.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Worldwide competitive programming contest for university students

The **International Collegiate Programming Contest** (**ICPC**) is an annual multi-tiered [competitive programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competitive_programming "Competitive programming") competition among the [universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University "University") of the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-CACM-1) Directed by ICPC Executive Director and [Baylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University") Professor William B. Poucher, the ICPC operates autonomous regional contests covering six continents culminating in a global World Finals every year. In 2018, ICPC participation included 52,709 students from 3,233 universities in 110 countries.

The ICPC operates under the auspices of the ICPC Foundation and operates under agreements with host universities and non-profits, all in accordance with the ICPC Policies and Procedures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-icpcpp-2) From 1977 until 2017 ICPC was held under the auspices of [ACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_Computing_Machinery "Association for Computing Machinery") and was referred to as ACM-ICPC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The ICPC traces its roots to a competition held at [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") in 1970 hosted by the Alpha chapter of the [Upsilon Pi Epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upsilon_Pi_Epsilon "Upsilon Pi Epsilon") Computer Science Honor Society (UPE). This initial programming competition was titled First Annual Texas Collegiate Programming Championship and each university was represented by a team of up to five members. The computer used was a [IBM System/360 model 65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_System_360 "IBM System 360") which was one of the first machines with a DAT (Dynamic Address Translator aka "paging") system for accessing memory. Teams that participated included Texas A&M, Texas Tech, University of Houston, and five or six other Texas University / Colleges. There were three problems that had to be completed and the cumulative time from "start" to "successful completion" determined first-, second-, and third-place winners. The programming language used was [Fortran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortran "Fortran"). The programs were written on coding sheets, keypunched on [Hollerith cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollerith_card "Hollerith card"), and submitted for execution. The [University of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Houston "University of Houston") team won the competition completing all three problems successfully with time. The second- and third-place teams did not successfully complete all three problems. The contest evolved into its present form as a multi-tier competition in 1977, with the first finals held in conjunction with the ACM Computer Science Conference.

From 1977 to 1989, the contest included mainly teams of four from universities throughout the United States and Canada. ICPC Headquarters was hosted by [Baylor University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University") from 1989 until 2022, with regional contests established within the world's university community, the ICPC has grown into a worldwide competition. To increase access to the World Finals, teams were reduced to three students within their first five academic years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From 1997 to 2017, [International Business Machines Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") (IBM) was the sponsor of ICPC. During that time contest participation has grown by more than 2000%. In 1997, 840 teams from 560 universities participated. In 2017, 46,381 students from 2,948 universities in 103 countries on six continents participated in regional competitions. Organized as a highly localized extra-curricular university mind sport and operating as a globally-coordinated unincorporated association operating under agreements with host universities and non-profits, the ICPC is open to qualified teams from every university in the world.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

UPE has provided continuous support since 1970 and honored World Finalists since the first Finals in 1976. The ICPC is indebted to ACM member contributions and ACM assistance from 1976 to 2018. Baylor University served since 1985, hosting ICPC Headquarters from 1989 until 2022. The ICPC operates under the auspices of the ICPC Foundation which provides the ICPC Global Headquarters to service a globally-coordinated community whose events operate under agreements with host universities and non-profits to insure that participation in ICPC is open to qualified teams from every university in the world. See ICPC Policies and Procedures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-icpcpp-2)

The ICPC World Finals (The Annual World Finals of the International Collegiate Programming Contest) is the final round of competition. Over its history it has become a 4-day event held in the finest venues worldwide with 140 teams competing in the 2018 World Finals. Recent World Champion teams have been recognized by their country's head of state. In recent years, media impressions have hovered at the one billion mark.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From 2000 to 2022, excluding 2021, only teams from [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") have won the ICPC world finals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-4) Participation in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") is much smaller than in the rest of the world, which is partially attributed to the perceived low payoff of participating.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-sigcse16-5)

## Contest rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contest rules")]

ICPC contests are team competitions. Current rules stipulate that each team consist of three students. Participants must be university students, who have had less than five years of university education before the contest. Students who have previously competed in two World Finals or five regional competitions are ineligible to compete again.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-7)

During each contest, the teams of three are given 5 hours to solve between eight and fifteen programming problems (with eight typical for regionals and twelve for finals). They must submit solutions as programs in [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)"), [C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++ "C++"), [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(programming_language) "Java (programming language)"), [Ada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_(programming_language) "Ada (programming language)"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-8)[Python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) "Python (programming language)")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-10) or [Kotlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotlin_(programming_language) "Kotlin (programming language)")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-11) (although it is not guaranteed every problem is solvable in any certain language, the ICPC website states that "the judges will have solved all problems in Java and C++" for both regional and world finals competitions). Programs are then run on test data. If a program fails to give a correct answer, the team is notified and can submit another program.

The winner is the team which correctly solves the most problems. If necessary to rank teams for medals or prizes among tying teams, the placement of teams is determined by the sum of the elapsed times at each point that they submitted correct solutions plus 20 minutes for each rejected submission of a problem ultimately solved. There is no time consumed for a problem that is not solved.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-12)

Compared to other programming contests (for example, [International Olympiad in Informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympiad_in_Informatics "International Olympiad in Informatics")), the ICPC is characterized by a large number of problems (eight or more problems in just 5 hours). Another feature is that each team can use only one computer, although teams have three students. This makes the time pressure even greater. Good teamwork and ability to withstand pressure is needed to win.

## 2004–2025 finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2004–2025 finals")]

### 2004 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2004 World Finals")]

The 2004 ACM-ICPC World Finals were hosted at the Obecni Dum, [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"), by [Czech Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Technical_University "Czech Technical University") in Prague. 3,150 teams representing 1,411 universities from 75 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 73 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics from Russia won, solving 7 of 10 problems.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-13) Gold medalists were St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics, [KTH Royal Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTH_Royal_Institute_of_Technology "KTH Royal Institute of Technology") (Sweden), Belarusian State University, and Perm State University (Russia).

### 2005 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2005 World Finals")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg/250px-ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg)

Opening Ceremony in 2005

The 2005 world finals were held at Pudong Shangri-La Hotel in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai") on April 6, 2005, hosted by [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University"). 4,109 teams representing 1,582 universities from 71 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 78 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") won its second world title, with 8 of 10 problems solved.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-14) Gold medal winners were Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Moscow State University (Russia), St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics (Russia), and University of Waterloo (Canada).

### 2006 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2006 World Finals")]

The 2006 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), and hosted by [Baylor University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-Sullivan-15) 5,606 teams representing 1,733 universities from 84 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 83 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. [Saratov State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratov_State_University "Saratov State University") from Russia won, solving 6 of 10 problems.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-16) Gold medal winners were Saratov, Jagiellonian University (Poland), Altai State Technical University (Russia), University of Twente (The Netherlands).

### 2007 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2007 World Finals")]

The 2007 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held at the Tokyo Bay Hilton, in Tokyo, Japan, March 12–16, 2007. The World Finals was hosted by the ACM Japan Chapter and the IBM Tokyo Research Lab. Some 6,099 teams competed on six continents at the regional level. Eighty-eight teams advanced to the World Finals. [Warsaw University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_University "Warsaw University") won its second world championship, solving 8 of 10 problems. Gold Medal Winners were Warsaw University, Tsinghua University (China), St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics (Russia), and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (United States). Silver Medal Winners include [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") (China) and 3 other universities.

### 2008 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2008 World Finals")]

The 2008 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held at the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, in Banff, Alberta, Canada, April 6–10, 2008.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-earthtimes-17) The World Finals was hosted by the University of Alberta. There were 100 teams in the World finals, out of 6700 total teams competing in the earlier rounds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-18) The [St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_Institute_of_Fine_Mechanics_and_Optics "St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics") won their second world championship. [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), [Izhevsk State Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izhevsk_State_Technical_University "Izhevsk State Technical University"), and [Lviv National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv_University "Lviv University") also received gold medals.

### 2009 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2009 World Finals")]

The 2009 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in Stockholm, Sweden, April 18–22, at the campus of the hosting institution, [KTH Royal Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTH_Royal_Institute_of_Technology "KTH Royal Institute of Technology"), as well as at the Grand Hotel, the Radisson Strand, and the Diplomat Hotel. There were 100 teams from over 200 regional sites competing for the World Championship. The [St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_Institute_of_Fine_Mechanics_and_Optics "St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics") defended their title, winning their third world championship. [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"), [St. Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_State_University "St. Petersburg State University"), and [Saratov State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratov_State_University "Saratov State University") also received gold medals.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-19) The 2009 World Finals pioneered live video broadcasting of the entire contest, featuring elements such as expert commentary, live feeds of teams and their computer screens and interviews with judges, coaches and dignitaries. The event was broadcast online, as well as by Swedish television channel [Axess TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axess_TV "Axess TV").

### 2010 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2010 World Finals")]

The 2010 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in [Harbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbin "Harbin"), China. The host is [Harbin Engineering University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbin_Engineering_University "Harbin Engineering University"). [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") won the world championship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-20)[Moscow State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_University "Moscow State University"), [National Taiwan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Taiwan_University "National Taiwan University"), and [Taras Shevchenko Kyiv National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiev_University "Kiev University") also received gold medals.

### 2011 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2011 World Finals")]

The 2011 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in Orlando, Florida and hosted by main sponsor [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"). The contest was initially scheduled to be held in [Sharm el-Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharm_el-Sheikh "Sharm el-Sheikh"), [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") in February, but was moved due to the political instability associated with the [Arab Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Spring "Arab Spring"). [Zhejiang University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhejiang_University "Zhejiang University") took first place with the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan") at Ann Arbor, [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"), and [Saint Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg_State_University "Saint Petersburg State University") taking 2nd, 3rd, and 4th respectively each receiving gold medals.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-21) China (2G) United States (1G) Russia (1G, 2S, 2B) Germany (1S) Ukraine (1S) Poland (1B) Canada (1B)

### 2012 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2012 World Finals")]

The 2012 World Finals were held in Warsaw, Poland. They were inaugurated on 15 May and hosted by [University of Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warsaw "University of Warsaw").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-22)[St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_Institute_of_Fine_Mechanics_and_Optics "St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics") won their fourth world championship, the most by any University at the time. [University of Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warsaw "University of Warsaw"), [Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Institute_of_Physics_and_Technology "Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology"), and [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") took 2nd, 3rd, and 4th place respectively each receiving gold medals. Russia (2G, 1B) China (1G,1S) Poland (1G) United States (1S) Hong Kong (1S) Belarus (1S, 1B) Canada (1B) Japan (1B)

### 2013 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2013 World Finals")]

2013 top thirteen teams that received medals are:

Japan (1G) Russia (1G, 1S, 2B) China (1G, 1B) Taiwan (1G) Poland (1S, 1B) Ukraine (1S) Belarus (1S) United States (1B)

*   [National Taiwan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Taiwan_University "National Taiwan University") (GOLD, 4th Place),

### 2015 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 2015 World Finals")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/ITMO_team_2015_ACM_ICPC.jpg/330px-ITMO_team_2015_ACM_ICPC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ITMO_team_2015_ACM_ICPC.jpg)

ITMO team 2015

The 2015 World Finals were held in [Marrakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh "Marrakesh") ([Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")) during May 16–21, hosted by [Mohammed the Fifth University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_the_Fifth_University "Mohammed the Fifth University"), [Al Akhawayn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Akhawayn_University "Al Akhawayn University") and [Mundiapolis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundiapolis_Universit%C3%A9_Priv%C3%A9e?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mundiapolis Université Privée (page does not exist)"). The final competition took place on May 20. 128 teams competed to be World Champion. Saint Petersburg ITMO emerged as the winner, having solved all problems (13) for the first time ever. Other medalists included teams from Russia (2G), China (1G, 1B, 1S), Japan (1G), the United States (1B, 1S), Croatia (1S), Czech Republic (1S), Korea (1B), and Poland (1B).

### 2016 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 2016 World Finals")]

The 2016 World Finals were held in [Phuket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phuket "Phuket") ([Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand")) during May 16–21. ### World Finals Luxor (2022 & 2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: World Finals Luxor (2022 & 2023)")]

To synchronize with the schedule after all rescheduling because of [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") both 46-th and 47-th world finals were scheduled to take place in the same time in November 2023 in [Sharm El Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharm_El_Sheikh "Sharm El Sheikh"). Because of [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") and related safety concerns, it was rescheduled once again and finally happened in [Luxor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxor "Luxor") in April from 14th to 19 April 2024. To avoid confusion about dates, the event was referred to as World Finals Luxor (World Finals Sharm before rescheduling), with two competitions as 46th and 47th separately, if needed, in all official materials.

Two competitions were held in parallel, with intersecting problem sets. In 47-th finals, due to very close results (less than 40 penalty minutes difference between 12 and 16 place), additional bronze medals were awarded at the next finals in Astana.

### World Finals Baku (2025)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: World Finals Baku (2025)")]

The 49th ICPC World Championship was held in [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku"), [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), from August 31 to September 5, 2025, hosted by [ADA University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADA_University "ADA University") in partnership with the [Central Bank of Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Azerbaijan "Central Bank of Azerbaijan").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-39)

139 teams competed to be World Champion. The winners were [Saint Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg_State_University "Saint Petersburg State University") team named Polar Bear Transform. They solved 11 out of 12 problems. With only two minutes left on the contest ending, the team submitted the final problem's solution that sealed their victory. Gold medals also went to the teams from Japan and China: The University of Tokyo, Beijing Jiaotong University, and Tsinghua University.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Worldwide competitive programming contest for university students

The **International Collegiate Programming Contest** (**ICPC**) is an annual multi-tiered [competitive programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competitive_programming "Competitive programming") competition among the [universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University "University") of the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-CACM-1) Directed by ICPC Executive Director and [Baylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University") Professor William B. Poucher, the ICPC operates autonomous regional contests covering six continents culminating in a global World Finals every year. In 2018, ICPC participation included 52,709 students from 3,233 universities in 110 countries.

The ICPC operates under the auspices of the ICPC Foundation and operates under agreements with host universities and non-profits, all in accordance with the ICPC Policies and Procedures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-icpcpp-2) From 1977 until 2017 ICPC was held under the auspices of [ACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_Computing_Machinery "Association for Computing Machinery") and was referred to as ACM-ICPC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The ICPC traces its roots to a competition held at [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University") in 1970 hosted by the Alpha chapter of the [Upsilon Pi Epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upsilon_Pi_Epsilon "Upsilon Pi Epsilon") Computer Science Honor Society (UPE). This initial programming competition was titled First Annual Texas Collegiate Programming Championship and each university was represented by a team of up to five members. The computer used was a [IBM System/360 model 65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_System_360 "IBM System 360") which was one of the first machines with a DAT (Dynamic Address Translator aka "paging") system for accessing memory. Teams that participated included Texas A&M, Texas Tech, University of Houston, and five or six other Texas University / Colleges. There were three problems that had to be completed and the cumulative time from "start" to "successful completion" determined first-, second-, and third-place winners. The programming language used was [Fortran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortran "Fortran"). The programs were written on coding sheets, keypunched on [Hollerith cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollerith_card "Hollerith card"), and submitted for execution. The [University of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Houston "University of Houston") team won the competition completing all three problems successfully with time. The second- and third-place teams did not successfully complete all three problems. The contest evolved into its present form as a multi-tier competition in 1977, with the first finals held in conjunction with the ACM Computer Science Conference.

From 1977 to 1989, the contest included mainly teams of four from universities throughout the United States and Canada. ICPC Headquarters was hosted by [Baylor University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University") from 1989 until 2022, with regional contests established within the world's university community, the ICPC has grown into a worldwide competition. To increase access to the World Finals, teams were reduced to three students within their first five academic years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From 1997 to 2017, [International Business Machines Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") (IBM) was the sponsor of ICPC. During that time contest participation has grown by more than 2000%. In 1997, 840 teams from 560 universities participated. In 2017, 46,381 students from 2,948 universities in 103 countries on six continents participated in regional competitions. Organized as a highly localized extra-curricular university mind sport and operating as a globally-coordinated unincorporated association operating under agreements with host universities and non-profits, the ICPC is open to qualified teams from every university in the world.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

UPE has provided continuous support since 1970 and honored World Finalists since the first Finals in 1976. The ICPC is indebted to ACM member contributions and ACM assistance from 1976 to 2018. Baylor University served since 1985, hosting ICPC Headquarters from 1989 until 2022. The ICPC operates under the auspices of the ICPC Foundation which provides the ICPC Global Headquarters to service a globally-coordinated community whose events operate under agreements with host universities and non-profits to insure that participation in ICPC is open to qualified teams from every university in the world. See ICPC Policies and Procedures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-icpcpp-2)

The ICPC World Finals (The Annual World Finals of the International Collegiate Programming Contest) is the final round of competition. Over its history it has become a 4-day event held in the finest venues worldwide with 140 teams competing in the 2018 World Finals. Recent World Champion teams have been recognized by their country's head of state. In recent years, media impressions have hovered at the one billion mark.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From 2000 to 2022, excluding 2021, only teams from [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") have won the ICPC world finals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-4) Participation in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") is much smaller than in the rest of the world, which is partially attributed to the perceived low payoff of participating.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-sigcse16-5)

## Contest rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contest rules")]

ICPC contests are team competitions. Current rules stipulate that each team consist of three students. Participants must be university students, who have had less than five years of university education before the contest. Students who have previously competed in two World Finals or five regional competitions are ineligible to compete again.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-7)

During each contest, the teams of three are given 5 hours to solve between eight and fifteen programming problems (with eight typical for regionals and twelve for finals). They must submit solutions as programs in [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)"), [C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++ "C++"), [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(programming_language) "Java (programming language)"), [Ada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_(programming_language) "Ada (programming language)"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-8)[Python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) "Python (programming language)")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-10) or [Kotlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotlin_(programming_language) "Kotlin (programming language)")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-11) (although it is not guaranteed every problem is solvable in any certain language, the ICPC website states that "the judges will have solved all problems in Java and C++" for both regional and world finals competitions). Programs are then run on test data. If a program fails to give a correct answer, the team is notified and can submit another program.

The winner is the team which correctly solves the most problems. If necessary to rank teams for medals or prizes among tying teams, the placement of teams is determined by the sum of the elapsed times at each point that they submitted correct solutions plus 20 minutes for each rejected submission of a problem ultimately solved. There is no time consumed for a problem that is not solved.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-12)

Compared to other programming contests (for example, [International Olympiad in Informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympiad_in_Informatics "International Olympiad in Informatics")), the ICPC is characterized by a large number of problems (eight or more problems in just 5 hours). Another feature is that each team can use only one computer, although teams have three students. This makes the time pressure even greater. Good teamwork and ability to withstand pressure is needed to win.

## 2004–2025 finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2004–2025 finals")]

### 2004 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2004 World Finals")]

The 2004 ACM-ICPC World Finals were hosted at the Obecni Dum, [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"), by [Czech Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Technical_University "Czech Technical University") in Prague. 3,150 teams representing 1,411 universities from 75 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 73 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics from Russia won, solving 7 of 10 problems.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-13) Gold medalists were St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics, [KTH Royal Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTH_Royal_Institute_of_Technology "KTH Royal Institute of Technology") (Sweden), Belarusian State University, and Perm State University (Russia).

### 2005 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2005 World Finals")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg/250px-ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ACM_ICPC_2005_Opening_Ceremony.jpg)

Opening Ceremony in 2005

The 2005 world finals were held at Pudong Shangri-La Hotel in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai") on April 6, 2005, hosted by [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University"). 4,109 teams representing 1,582 universities from 71 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 78 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") won its second world title, with 8 of 10 problems solved.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-14) Gold medal winners were Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Moscow State University (Russia), St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics (Russia), and University of Waterloo (Canada).

### 2006 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2006 World Finals")]

The 2006 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), and hosted by [Baylor University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University "Baylor University").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-Sullivan-15) 5,606 teams representing 1,733 universities from 84 countries competed in elimination rounds, with 83 of those teams proceeding to the world finals. [Saratov State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratov_State_University "Saratov State University") from Russia won, solving 6 of 10 problems.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-16) Gold medal winners were Saratov, Jagiellonian University (Poland), Altai State Technical University (Russia), University of Twente (The Netherlands).

### 2007 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2007 World Finals")]

The 2007 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held at the Tokyo Bay Hilton, in Tokyo, Japan, March 12–16, 2007. The World Finals was hosted by the ACM Japan Chapter and the IBM Tokyo Research Lab. Some 6,099 teams competed on six continents at the regional level. Eighty-eight teams advanced to the World Finals. [Warsaw University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_University "Warsaw University") won its second world championship, solving 8 of 10 problems. Gold Medal Winners were Warsaw University, Tsinghua University (China), St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics (Russia), and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (United States). Silver Medal Winners include [Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") (China) and 3 other universities.

### 2008 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2008 World Finals")]

The 2008 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held at the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, in Banff, Alberta, Canada, April 6–10, 2008.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-earthtimes-17) The World Finals was hosted by the University of Alberta. There were 100 teams in the World finals, out of 6700 total teams competing in the earlier rounds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-18) The [St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_Institute_of_Fine_Mechanics_and_Optics "St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics") won their second world championship. [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), [Izhevsk State Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izhevsk_State_Technical_University "Izhevsk State Technical University"), and [Lviv National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv_University "Lviv University") also received gold medals.

### 2009 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2009 World Finals")]

The 2009 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in Stockholm, Sweden, April 18–22, at the campus of the hosting institution, [KTH Royal Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTH_Royal_Institute_of_Technology "KTH Royal Institute of Technology"), as well as at the Grand Hotel, the Radisson Strand, and the Diplomat Hotel. There were 100 teams from over 200 regional sites competing for the World Championship. The [St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_Institute_of_Fine_Mechanics_and_Optics "St. Petersburg Institute of Fine Mechanics and Optics") defended their title, winning their third world championship. [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"), [St. Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg_State_University "St. Petersburg State University"), and [Saratov State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratov_State_University "Saratov State University") also received gold medals.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-19) The 2009 World Finals pioneered live video broadcasting of the entire contest, featuring elements such as expert commentary, live feeds of teams and their computer screens and interviews with judges, coaches and dignitaries. The event was broadcast online, as well as by Swedish television channel [Axess TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axess_TV "Axess TV").

[Shanghai Jiao Tong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Jiao_Tong_University "Shanghai Jiao Tong University") won the world championship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-20)[Moscow State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_University "Moscow State University"), [National Taiwan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Taiwan_University "National Taiwan University"), and [Taras Shevchenko Kyiv National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiev_University "Kiev University") also received gold medals.

### 2011 World Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2011 World Finals")]

The 2011 ACM-ICPC World Finals were held in Orlando, Florida and hosted by main sponsor [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"). The contest was initially scheduled to be held in [Sharm el-Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharm_el-Sheikh "Sharm el-Sheikh"), [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") in February, but was moved due to the political instability associated with the [Arab Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Spring "Arab Spring"). [Zhejiang University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhejiang_University "Zhejiang University") took first place with the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan") at Ann Arbor, [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"), and [Saint Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg_State_University "Saint Petersburg State University") taking 2nd, 3rd, and 4th respectively each receiving gold medals.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-21) China (2G) United States (1G) Russia (1G, 2S, 2B) Germany (1S) Ukraine (1S) Poland (1B) Canada (1B)

### World Finals Luxor (2022 & 2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: World Finals Luxor (2022 & 2023)")]

To synchronize with the schedule after all rescheduling because of [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") both 46-th and 47-th world finals were scheduled to take place in the same time in November 2023 in [Sharm El Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharm_El_Sheikh "Sharm El Sheikh"). Because of [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") and related safety concerns, it was rescheduled once again and finally happened in [Luxor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxor "Luxor") in April from 14th to 19 April 2024. To avoid confusion about dates, the event was referred to as World Finals Luxor (World Finals Sharm before rescheduling), with two competitions as 46th and 47th separately, if needed, in all official materials.

Two competitions were held in parallel, with intersecting problem sets. In 47-th finals, due to very close results (less than 40 penalty minutes difference between 12 and 16 place), additional bronze medals were awarded at the next finals in Astana.

### World Finals Baku (2025)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: World Finals Baku (2025)")]

The 49th ICPC World Championship was held in [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku"), [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), from August 31 to September 5, 2025, hosted by [ADA University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADA_University "ADA University") in partnership with the [Central Bank of Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Azerbaijan "Central Bank of Azerbaijan").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest#cite_note-39)

139 teams competed to be World Champion. The winners were [Saint Petersburg State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg_State_University "Saint Petersburg State University") team named Polar Bear Transform. They solved 11 out of 12 problems. With only two minutes left on the contest ending, the team submitted the final problem's solution that sealed their victory. Gold medals also went to the teams from Japan and China: The University of Tokyo, Beijing Jiaotong University, and Tsinghua University.
