The first buildings of the campus, which make up what are now known as the Main Quadrangles, were part of a master plan conceived by two University of Chicago trustees and plotted by Chicago architect [Henry Ives Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ives_Cobb "Henry Ives Cobb").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37) The Main Quadrangles consist of six [quadrangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrangle_(architecture) "Quadrangle (architecture)"), each surrounded by buildings, bordering one larger quadrangle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-goodspeed-11):221 The buildings of the Main Quadrangles were designed by Cobb, [Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepley,_Rutan_and_Coolidge "Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge"), [Holabird & Roche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holabird_&_Roche "Holabird & Roche"), and other architectural firms in a mixture of the [Victorian Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_Gothic "Victorian Gothic") and [Collegiate Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Gothic "Collegiate Gothic") styles, patterned on the colleges of the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37) Mitchell Tower, for example, is modeled after Oxford's [Magdalen Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_Tower "Magdalen Tower"),[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-mitchell-38) and the university Commons, [Hutchinson Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutchinson_Hall "Hutchinson Hall"), replicates [Christ Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Oxford "Christ Church, Oxford") Hall.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-39) In celebration of the 2018 Illinois Bicentennial, the University of Chicago Quadrangles were selected as one of the Illinois 200 Great Places by the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") Illinois component.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-41)

[![Image 15: A comparison between the similar architectures of Chicago's Mitchell Tower on the left and Oxford's Magdalen Tower on the right.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Mitchell-Magdalen_comparison.jpg/250px-Mitchell-Magdalen_comparison.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mitchell-Magdalen_comparison.jpg)

Many older buildings of the University of Chicago employ [Collegiate Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Gothic "Collegiate Gothic") architecture like that of the University of Oxford. For example, Chicago's Mitchell Tower (left) was modeled after Oxford's [Magdalen Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_Tower,_Oxford "Magdalen Tower, Oxford") (right).

After the 1940s, the campus's Gothic style began to give way to modern styles.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37) In 1955, [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen") was contracted to develop a second master plan, which led to the construction of buildings both north and south of the Midway, including the Laird Bell Law Quadrangle (a complex designed by Saarinen);[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37) a series of arts buildings;[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37) Edith Abbott Hall, designed by [Ludwig Mies van der Rohe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Mies_van_der_Rohe "Ludwig Mies van der Rohe");[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-42) the Keller Center, which is home of the [Harris School of Public Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Harris_School_of_Public_Policy "University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy") and was designed by Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenstein_Library "Regenstein Library"), the largest building on campus, a [brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture") structure designed by [Walter Netsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Netsch "Walter Netsch").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-44) Another master plan, designed in 1999 and updated in 2004,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-twentytwenty-45) produced the [Gerald Ratner Athletics Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ratner_Athletics_Center "Gerald Ratner Athletics Center") (2003),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-twentytwenty-45) the [Max Palevsky Residential Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Palevsky_Residential_Commons "Max Palevsky Residential Commons") (2001),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-famousbldgs-37)[South Campus Residence Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Campus_Residence_Hall "South Campus Residence Hall") and dining commons (2009), a new children's hospital,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-milestones-46) and other construction, expansions, and The site of [Chicago Pile-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Pile-1 "Chicago Pile-1") is a [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") and is marked by the [Henry Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moore "Henry Moore") sculpture _[Nuclear Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear\_Energy\_(sculpture) "Nuclear Energy (sculpture)")_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-49)[Robie House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robie_House "Robie House"), a [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lloyd_Wright "Frank Lloyd Wright") building acquired by the university in 1963, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-51) as well as a National Historic Landmark,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-52) as is room 405 of the [George Herbert Jones Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Herbert_Jones_Laboratory "George Herbert Jones Laboratory"), where [Glenn T. Seaborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_T._Seaborg "Glenn T. Seaborg") and his team were the first to isolate plutonium.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-53)[Hitchcock Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitchcock_Hall "Hitchcock Hall"), an undergraduate dormitory, is on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-nrhp-54)

Adjacent to the campus in [Jackson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Park_(Chicago) "Jackson Park (Chicago)") is the home of the [Obama Presidential Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama_Presidential_Center "Barack Obama Presidential Center"), the Presidential Library for the 44th president of the United States[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-55) that was officially opened in 2026.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-56) The Obamas settled in the university's Hyde Park neighborhood, where they raised their children and where [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") began his political career. #### Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Transportation")]

[![Image 20: Two University of Chicago shuttle buses (with "UGo" red branding on the sides) on 57th Street outside the Regenstein Library during a snowstorm](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/UChicago_UGo_Busses_in_Snow.png/250px-UChicago_UGo_Busses_in_Snow.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UChicago_UGo_Busses_in_Snow.png)

Two University of Chicago shuttle buses on 57th Street outside [Regenstein Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenstein_Library "Regenstein Library")

The Hyde Park campus is served by the CTA [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(CTA) "Red Line (CTA)") and [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(CTA) "Green Line (CTA)"), as well as by the [Metra Electric District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metra_Electric_District "Metra Electric District"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:73-60) all of which provide access to downtown Chicago.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-63) The [South Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Line "South Shore Line") provides access to [Hegeswich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegeswich "Hegeswich") and [Northwest Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Indiana "Northwest Indiana") via the [Lakeshore Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeshore_Corridor "Lakeshore Corridor").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-64) The campus is also served by a network of [CTA bus routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTA_bus_routes "CTA bus routes").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:73-60)

The university shuttle program includes daytime and nighttime routes, most of which operate within Hyde Park.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:82-65) In 2022, the university added a Downtown Campus Connector to its shuttle program, which connects the main Hyde Park campus to the Gleacher Center and downtown UChicago Medicine clinics.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-66)

In 2024, the university introduced a [Via](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Transportation "Via Transportation") ride-sharing program ahead of the 2024–2025 school year, which provides unlimited free rides on campus in shared vans.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-67)

#### Safety

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Safety")]

In November 2021, a university graduate was robbed and fatally shot on a sidewalk in a residential area in Hyde Park near campus; a total of three University of Chicago students were killed by gunfire incidents in 2021.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-Suspect_Charged-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-could_be_anyone-69) These incidents prompted student protests and an open letter to university leadership signed by more than 300 faculty members.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-71) In response, the university introduced measures including increased foot and vehicular patrols near campus, expanded coordination between the [university police department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Police_Department "University Police Department") and the [Chicago Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Police_Department "Chicago Police Department"), and greater use of [security cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-circuit_television "Closed-circuit television") and [license plate readers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_number-plate_recognition "Automatic number-plate recognition").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-72) The university continues to maintain one of the largest private police forces in the country.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-73)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Academics")]

[![Image 22: A large gate, with students walking through](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/University_of_Chicago_July_2013_19_%28Main_Quadrangles%29.jpg/250px-University_of_Chicago_July_2013_19_%28Main_Quadrangles%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Chicago_July_2013_19_(Main_Quadrangles).jpg)

The University of Chicago Main Quadrangles, looking north

The academic bodies of the University of Chicago consist of the [college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_University_of_Chicago "College of the University of Chicago"), four divisions of graduate research, seven professional schools, and the [Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_School_of_Continuing_Liberal_and_Professional_Studies "Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-80) The university also contains a library system, the [University of Chicago Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Press "University of Chicago Press"), and the [University of Chicago Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Medical_Center "University of Chicago Medical Center"), and oversees several laboratories, including the [Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermilab "Fermilab") (Fermilab), the [Argonne National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonne_National_Laboratory "Argonne National Laboratory"), and the [Marine Biological Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Biological_Laboratory "Marine Biological Laboratory").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:5-81) The university is accredited by the [Higher Learning Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Higher_Learning_Commission "The Higher Learning Commission").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-collegenavigator-82) It is a member of the [National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Independent_Colleges_and_Universities "National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities") and the [Universities Research Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_Research_Association "Universities Research Association").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-84)

The university runs on a [quarter system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_system "Quarter system") in which the academic year is divided into four terms: Summer (June–August), Autumn (September–December), Winter (January–March), and Spring (March–June).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:10-85) Full-time undergraduate students take three to four courses every quarter[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-86) for approximately ten weeks before their quarterly academic breaks. The school year typically begins in late September and ends in early June.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:10-85)

### Undergraduate college

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Undergraduate college")]

Main article: [College of the University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_University_of_Chicago "College of the University of Chicago")

[![Image 23: The campus in winter, with snow covering the ground](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Harper_Library_from_the_Midway_Plaisance.JPG/250px-Harper_Library_from_the_Midway_Plaisance.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harper_Library_from_the_Midway_Plaisance.JPG)

Harper Memorial Library was dedicated in 1912, and its architecture takes inspiration from various colleges in England.

The College of the University of Chicago grants Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Science degrees in 51 undergraduate majors and 33 minors.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-87) The college's academics are divided into five divisions: the Biological Sciences Collegiate Division, the Physical Sciences Collegiate Division, the Social Sciences Collegiate Division, the Humanities Collegiate Division, and the New Collegiate Division.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-88) Each division, except for the interdisciplinary New Collegiate Division, is affiliated with the corresponding graduate division of the university.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-90)

The college introduced a now-widespread model of the liberal arts undergraduate program which featured the [Socratic method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socratic_method "Socratic method") in undergraduate contexts, the [Great Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Books_of_the_Western_World#History "Great Books of the Western World") program, and the [core curriculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_curriculum "Core curriculum").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-93) Since the 1999–2000 school year, 15 courses across seven subjects and demonstrated proficiency in a foreign language are required under the core curriculum.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:6-94)

[![Image 24: A large building](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Eckhart_Hall.jpg/250px-Eckhart_Hall.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eckhart_Hall.jpg)

Eckhart Hall houses the university's math department.

### Graduate research divisions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Graduate research divisions")]

The university's academic departments, committees, and institutes are organized into four graduate research divisions: the Arts & Humanities Division, the Biological Sciences Division, the Physical Sciences Division, and the Social Sciences Division.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-95)

In the autumn quarter of 2022, the university enrolled 10,546 graduate students on degree-seeking courses: 569 in the Biological Sciences Division, 612 in the Humanities Division, 2,103 in the Physical Sciences Division, 972 in the Social Sciences Division, and 6,290 in the professional schools (including the Graham School).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-96) The university is home to several committees for interdisciplinary scholarship, including the [Committee on Social Thought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_on_Social_Thought "Committee on Social Thought").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-97)

According to the [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), the University of Chicago spent $423.9 million on research and development in 2018, ranking it 60th in the nation.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-98) It is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-99) It is a founding member of the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities"), and was a member of the Committee on Institutional Cooperation between 1946 and 2016, when the group's name was changed to the [Big Ten Academic Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Academic_Alliance "Big Ten Academic Alliance"). The University of Chicago is not a member of the rebranded consortium, but continues to be a collaborator.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-btaa_chicago-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-101)

The university operates more than 140 research centers and institutes on campus. Among these are the [Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, West Asia & North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_the_Study_of_Ancient_Cultures "Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures")—a museum and research center for [Near Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_East "Near East") studies owned and operated by the university—and a number of [National Resource Centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Resource_Center "National Resource Center"), including the [Center for Middle Eastern Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Middle_Eastern_Studies_at_the_University_of_Chicago "Center for Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Chicago").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-102) Chicago also operates or is affiliated with several research institutions apart from the university proper. The university manages the [Argonne National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonne_National_Laboratory "Argonne National Laboratory"), part of the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy")'s national laboratory system, and co-manages the [Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermilab "Fermilab") (Fermilab), a nearby particle physics laboratory.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-:5-81) It was also part of the Astrophysical Research Consortium that constructed the [Apache Point Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Point_Observatory "Apache Point Observatory") in [Sunspot, New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunspot,_New_Mexico "Sunspot, New Mexico").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-103) Faculty and students at the adjacent [Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Technological_Institute_at_Chicago "Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago") collaborate with the university.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-104) In 2013, the university formed an affiliation with the formerly independent [Marine Biological Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Biological_Laboratory "Marine Biological Laboratory") in Woods Hole, Mass.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-105) The [National Opinion Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Opinion_Research_Center "National Opinion Research Center") maintains an office at the Hyde Park campus and is affiliated with multiple academic centers and institutes.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-107)

[![Image 26: Ivy-colored building with various shades of color](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/University_of_Chicago_at_Fall.jpg/250px-University_of_Chicago_at_Fall.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Chicago_at_Fall.jpg)

University of Chicago building during fall

The University of Chicago has been the site of various experiments and academic movements. The university has played a role in shaping ideas about the [free market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market")[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-108) and is the namesake of the [Chicago school of economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_school_of_economics "Chicago school of economics"), the school of economic thought supported by [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman "Milton Friedman") and other economists. The university's [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology") department was the first independent sociology department in the United States and gave birth to the [Chicago school of sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_school_(sociology) "Chicago school (sociology)").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-109) The [Chicago school of mathematical analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_school_of_mathematical_analysis "Chicago school of mathematical analysis") is a [school of thought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_thought "School of thought") in mathematics that emphasizes the applications of [Fourier analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_analysis "Fourier analysis") to the study of [partial differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equations "Partial differential equations") and was founded at the Universty of Chicago in the 1950s.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-113) The university was the site of the [Chicago Pile-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Pile-1 "Chicago Pile-1") (the first controlled, self-sustaining human-made nuclear chain reaction, part of the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project")), of [Robert Millikan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Millikan "Robert Millikan")'s [oil-drop experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil-drop_experiment "Oil-drop experiment") that calculated the charge of the electron,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-oildrop-114) and of the development of [radiocarbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating "Radiocarbon dating") by [Willard F. Libby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willard_F._Libby "Willard F. Libby") in 1946.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-115) The chemical experiment that tested how life originated on early Earth, the [Miller–Urey experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Urey_experiment "Miller–Urey experiment"), was also conducted at the university.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-116)[REM sleep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REM_sleep "REM sleep") was discovered at the university in 1953 by [Nathaniel Kleitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Kleitman "Nathaniel Kleitman") and [Eugene Aserinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Aserinsky "Eugene Aserinsky").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-117)

The university contains seven professional schools, as well as the [Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_School_of_Continuing_Liberal_and_Professional_Studies "Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies").

It offers four graduate degree programs as well as undergraduate course offerings.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-120) It has been accredited by the [Association of Theological Schools in the United States and Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Theological_Schools_in_the_United_States_and_Canada "Association of Theological Schools in the United States and Canada") since 1938.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-collegenavigator2-121)

*   The [University of Chicago Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Law_School "University of Chicago Law School") was established in 1902, twelve years after the founding of the university.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-126) It has been accredited by the [American Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") since 1923 and was ranked third out of 195 American law schools by U.S. News in 2025.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-collegenavigator2-121)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-127)

It was renamed in 2021 in recognition of a $75 million donation from [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Crown "James Crown") and Paula Crown and the Crown family.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-129)
*   The [Pritzker School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_School_of_Medicine "Pritzker School of Medicine") matriculated its first class of medical students in 1927 and was renamed to the Pritzker School of Medicine in 1968 in recognition of support from the [Pritzker family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_family "Pritzker family").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-130) It has been accredited by the [Liaison Committee on Medical Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaison_Committee_on_Medical_Education "Liaison Committee on Medical Education") since 1942.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-collegenavigator2-121) In 2023, the school declined to continue submitting data to U.S. News to help the publication rank the institution, joining medical schools including those at Harvard, Stanford, and Columbia in doing so.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-131)

In 1990, it was renamed in recognition of [Irving Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Harris "Irving Harris")' financial support of the program during its inception.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-132) The school offers six graduate degree programs as well as joint degree and non-degree programs.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-133)
*   The [Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_School_of_Molecular_Engineering "Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering") was founded in 2019 following an expansion of the Institute of Molecular Engineering, which was established in 2011. The Pritzker Foundation provided a $75 million donation to help establish the school, which occupies the William Eckhardt Research Center.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-134)

Graham School of General Studies in honor of a $10 million donation from William and Catherine Graham made in the same year.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-137)

The Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts, opened in 2012

The University of Chicago Arts program joins academic departments in the Division of the Arts & Humanities and the undergraduate College, student art programs, and professional organizations including the [Court Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_Theatre_(Chicago) "Court Theatre (Chicago)"), the [Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_the_Study_of_Ancient_Cultures "Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures"), the [Smart Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_Museum_of_Art "Smart Museum of Art"), and the [Renaissance Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_Society "Renaissance Society").[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-157) The university offers graduate degrees in music, cinema and media studies, visual arts, and the humanities, among other subjects.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-158)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-159) It also offers bachelor's degree programs in visual arts, music, art history, cinema and media studies, and theater and performance studies.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-160) Several thousand major and non-major undergraduates enroll annually in creative and performing arts classes.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago#cite_note-161)

repeats, try a detail page or another supported route. Links outside the menu and inferred
paths on an observed site are allowed. Child notes are returned automatically;
do not copy their facts into your own note. Retain useful unvisited links even

# Timeline of the First 100 Years

1.   [Home](https://www.aaup.org/)
2.   [About](https://www.aaup.org/about)
3.   [History](https://www.aaup.org/about/history-aaup)
4.    Timeline 



When the American Association of University Professors was founded in January 1915, higher education bore little resemblance to the system that exists in this country today. The degrees awarded each year by America’s colleges and universities numbered in the tens of thousands rather than in the millions, and the student body was overwhelmingly white, male, and drawn from the social elite. Faculty members did not widely enjoy due-process protections; on the contrary, colleges and universities often operated under governments “of men and not of laws,” to quote from the AAUP’s first investigative report. Lacking tenure, the majority of faculty members at the time served on what would now be regarded as contingent appointments.

The creation of the AAUP was preceded by work undertaken in 1914 by the Joint Committee on Academic Freedom and Tenure, also known as the “committee of nine.” This committee, which included three representatives each from the American Economic Association, the American Sociological Society, and the American Political Science Association and was headed by Columbia University economics professor Edwin R. A. Seligman, was charged with examining academic freedom issues and investigating individual cases. The difficulties of undertaking this work through separate disciplinary societies made apparent the need for a more broadly conceived faculty association.

It was against this backdrop, and in the context of a larger movement toward the consolidation of professional identity through representative national organizations, that the AAUP was established.

The five illustrated banners and timeline below, prepared in 2015 in celebration of the AAUP's centennial, highlight key events in the AAUP's first century. Please note that the banners appear below in the form of large .pdf files, and there may be some delay in loading the images.

[Centennial banner 1915-1920](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/Banner1_Final2.pdf)  
[Centennial banner 1921-1955](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/Banner2_Final.pdf)  
[Centennial banner 1956-1969](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/Banner3_final.pdf)  
[Centennial banner 1970-2000](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/Banner4_Final.pdf)  
[Centennial banner 2001-2015](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/Banner5_Final2.pdf)

## Timeline: The AAUP’s First Century

**1915**The AAUP is founded at an organizational meeting held in New York City on January 1 and 2. At the meeting, John Dewey, a professor of education and psychology at Columbia University, takes office as the first president, and Arthur O. Lovejoy, a philosophy professor at Johns Hopkins University, becomes the first secretary. Dewey appoints Edwin R. A. Seligman, the economist who had led the joint “committee of nine,” to chair a committee charged with considering questions of academic freedom and tenure—a body that soon evolves into Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure.

_Listen to an [audio clip](https://www.aaup.org/about/history/aaup-archives#Organizing) in which Lovejoy discusses planning an organizing meeting in Baltimore that_ _preceded the public founding of the AAUP in New York and to [Lovejoy's account](https://www.aaup.org/about/history/aaup-archives#Dewey) of how he persuaded Dewey to serve as the AAUP's first president._
![Image 3](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/chemists3(1).jpg)  
The Chemists' Club, site of the meeting at which the AAUP was founded
In March 1915, seventeen faculty members at the University of Utah resign in protest after the appointments of four of their colleagues are abruptly terminated by the president and board of trustees. A month later, the AAUP, at Lovejoy’s urging, launches [an investigation](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/files/University%20of%20Utah%20-%20December%201915.pdf) into violations of principles of academic freedom and tenure at Utah—the first of five investigations that the new Association will undertake in its first year as it puts its principles into practice.

_Listen to a [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0apSikVwYN4 "(opens in a new window)") of Lovejoy recalling his role in launching the first investigation._
![Image 4](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/Scott_Nearing(1).jpg)  
  
Scott Nearing, an economics professor at the University of  
 Pennsylvania, came under fire from conservative alumni for his  
 public opposition to child labor. Nearing became the subject of  
 the AAUP’s fourth investigation after the board of trustees—  
 overruling the recommendation of the dean, department chair,  
 and faculty—chose not to renew his appointment.
A list of [“charter members”](https://archive.org/details/listofchartermem00amerrich "(opens in a new window)") published in May 1915 includes the names of more than nine hundred professors from sixty-one institutions. Membership is by nomination and election.
In December, the AAUP publishes [the inaugural volume of the _Bulletin of the American Association of University Professors_](http://www.jstor.org/stable/i40007593 "(opens in a new window)"). Included in the _Bulletin_ is the foundational statement now known as the 1915 _Declaration of Principles on Academic Freedom and Academic Tenure_, which states, “Once appointed, the scholar has professional functions to perform in which the appointing authorities have neither competency nor moral right to intervene. The responsibility of the university teacher is primarily to the public itself, and to the judgment of his own profession."
**1916**The AAUP adopts a resolution to create Committee T on the Place and Function of Faculties in University Government and Administration. This committee (now the Committee on College and University Governance) becomes central to the Association’s effort to promote a strong faculty role in the governance of higher education institutions.
![Image 5](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/map(2).jpg)  
Geographical distribution of AAUP members in early 1916
**1917**_The United States enters World War I._
The annual meeting votes to establish Committee W on the Status of Women in College and University Faculties “to report upon . . . the appointment of women to the higher academic positions; upon the opportunities for advancement now offered and that should be offered to women of ability and scholarship in the various fields of college and university teaching; and upon all other problems involved in the determination of the present or the desirable status of women in college and university faculties.”
**1918**_World War I ends._
**1919**Writing in his president’s message that economic circumstances in the United States following World War I had made it impossible “that this, the only general professional society of university teachers, should any longer ignore the economic side of the teacher’s calling,” Arthur O. Lovejoy announces the creation of the Committee on the Economic Condition of the Profession.
![Image 6](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/lovejoy1.jpg)  
Arthur O. Lovejoy
**1920**_The Nineteenth Amendment is ratified, giving women the right to vote._
**1925**The AAUP participates in the drafting of the _Conference Statement on Academic Freedom and Tenure_—the first jointly formulated statement to enumerate principles of academic freedom—at a meeting of higher education organizations.
**1928**AAUP members in Iowa establish the first state conference of AAUP chapters.
**1929**_The US stock market crashes, bringing the “roaring twenties” to a sudden end and marking the beginning of the decade-long Great Depression._
**1930**The AAUP’s national office is established. H. W. Tyler, a recently retired mathematics professor from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who had followed Lovejoy as second secretary of the Association and served in that capacity until 1930, heads the new office as general secretary.
![Image 7](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/tyler(3).jpg)  
H. W. Tyler
**1931**The AAUP’s membership exceeds ten thousand.
**1932**_Franklin Delano Roosevelt is elected president and pledges “a new deal for the American people.”_
![Image 8](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/einsteinfront(1).jpg)  
Albert Einstein’s AAUP membership card. Einstein was an AAUP member from 1935 until his death in 1955.
**1936**The nonreappointment of Jerome Davis, a long-serving professor at Yale Divinity School who had advocated for organized labor and other social causes, brings to the fore the need for a probationary period of standard length. Concern over this case and other, similar ones becomes a factor leading to the formulation of the 1940 _Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure_.
**1937**McGraw-Hill publishes _Depression, Recovery, and Higher Education_, a book-length report by a special committee of the AAUP that addresses the consequences of the Great Depression for faculty members, students, and institutions. The volume anticipates future reports on the economic status of the profession.
**1938**The AAUP establishes policies for formally censuring administrations for violations of principles of academic freedom and tenure and begins publishing censure lists in the _Bulletin_.
**1940**A series of joint conferences begun in the mid-1930s between the Association of American Colleges (now the Association of American Colleges and Universities) and the AAUP culminates in agreement on a reformulation of the principles laid out in the 1925 _Conference Statement on Academic Freedom and Tenure_. The resulting 1940 [_Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure_](https://www.aaup.org/report/1940-statement-principles-academic-freedom-and-tenure) defines faculty rights and responsibilities with regard to speech in the classroom, extramural speech, and research and establishes a maximum seven-year probationary period for tenure.
**1941**_The United States enters World War II after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor._
**1944**_The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944, commonly referred to as the GI Bill, is signed into law. Millions of veterans enter college in the years following the law’s passage, nearly doubling the student population._
![Image 9](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/Gibill(1).jpg)  
President Franklin Delano Roosevelt signs the GI Bill.
**1945**_World War II ends._
**1946**_The President’s Commission on Higher Education is charged with examining the role of higher education in postwar America. A year later, the resulting Truman Commission Report recommends a massive expansion of college enrollments and the establishment of a network of community colleges._
**1947**The AAUP’s membership exceeds twenty thousand.
**1948**The AAUP’s Committee on the Economic Status of the Profession publishes the results of its first survey of faculty salaries.
![Image 10](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/himstead.jpg)  
Ralph Himstead, the AAUP's general secretary from 1936 to 1955
**1949**After releasing an investigation of Evansville College (and declining to impose censure), the AAUP enters a period of relative inactivity.
**1954**_The US Supreme Court rules in_ Brown v. Board of Education _that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”_
![Image 11](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/annualmtg1954(1).jpg)  
A scene from the 1954 annual meeting
**1955**The election of new Council members and officers, together with changes in the AAUP’s national office, brings to an end the AAUP’s quiescence during the McCarthy era.
**1956**Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure issues the first part of _Academic Freedom and Tenure in the Quest for National Security_, an investigation of multiple cases that had been neglected in the preceding years. Unprecedented in its scope, the report does much to repair the Association’s reputation as a defender of academic freedom and due process.
**1957**Committee A formulates the first version of the [_Recommended Institutional Regulations on Academic Freedom and Tenure_](https://www.aaup.org/report/recommended-institutional-regulations-academic-freedom-and-tenure). These recommended regulations, derived from the Association’s key statements, are subsequently integrated into the policies of colleges and universities across the United States.
_The US Supreme Court upholds the right of Paul Sweezy, a university lecturer, to decline to answer questions posed by a state body investigating subversive activities. Justice Felix Frankfurter, in his concurrence in_ Sweezy v. New Hampshire _, establishes the constitutional doctrine of academic freedom when he cites “four essential freedoms of a university—to determine for itself on academic grounds who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted to study.”_
![Image 12](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/fuchs.jpg)  
Ralph F. Fuchs, the AAUP’s general secretary from 1955 to 1957
**1958**The AAUP enters the legal arena, filing its first amicus brief in the US Supreme Court on behalf of Lloyd Barenblatt, a University of Michigan teaching fellow who had refused to answer questions posed by the House Un-American Activities Committee.
**1959**The Council of State and Regional Conferences, the predecessor to the AAUP’s Assembly of State Conferences, is organized and holds its first meeting.
The annual meeting approves an amendment to the AAUP’s constitution that replaces the system of membership by nomination with one of membership by application; membership exceeds forty thousand.
**1960**Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure begins to address the issue of students’ academic freedom in response to what committee chair David Fellman describes as “events around the country, and particularly in the South” that confronted students “with many questions which in some fashion relate to their general claim to academic freedom,” including “students’ activities in connection with the desegregation controversy.”
Monmouth College and the University of Miami become the first institutions to be investigated by Committee T for infringements of governance standards.
![Image 13](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/1960%20bulletin%20ad.jpg)  
1960 advertisement for the AAUP
**1963**Faculty members at Nassau Community College form the first AAUP chapter on a community college campus.
**1964**_The Civil Rights Act becomes law._
**1965**The AAUP establishes a Special Committee on the Representation of Economic Interests to consider extending the activities of the Association into collective bargaining.
**1966**Professors at St. John’s University begin the first major US faculty strike over the administration’s summary dismissal of a group of their colleagues. The AAUP conducts an investigation into the administration’s actions but does not support the strike.
The AAUP issues its central policy document on the faculty’s role in governance, the 1966 [_Statement on Government of Colleges and Universities_](https://www.aaup.org/report/statement-government-colleges-and-universities). Formulated jointly by the AAUP, the American Council on Education, and the Association of Governing Boards of Universities and Colleges, the statement calls for cooperation among faculties, administrations, and governing boards and notes that the faculty should have “primary responsibility for such fundamental areas as curriculum, subject matter and methods of instruction, research, faculty status, and those aspects of student life which relate to the educational process.”
The AAUP issues the _[Statement on Professional Ethics](https://www.aaup.org/report/statement-professional-ethics)_,which delineates the responsibilities that accompany the rights of members of the academic profession.
**1967**In a development of which the national AAUP is initially unaware, faculty members at Belleville Area College (now Southwestern Illinois College) vote to designate their chapter as their exclusive representative in bargaining, making it the first AAUP collective bargaining chapter.
![Image 14](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/MLK.jpg)  
Martin Luther King Jr. speaks against the war in Vietnam at the Saint Paul campus of the University of Minnesota in April 1967. Photograph from the Minnesota Historical Society (CC BY-SA 2.0)
_The US Supreme Court holds in_ Keyishian v. Board of Regents _that states cannot terminate the appointments of faculty members on the basis of their refusal to sign a loyalty oath disavowing membership in the Communist Party. Justice William Brennan writes in his majority ruling: \_“\_ Our Nation is deeply committed to safeguarding academic freedom, which is of transcendent value to all of us and not merely to the teachers concerned. That freedom is therefore a special concern of the First Amendment, which does not tolerate laws that cast a pall of orthodoxy over the classroom.\_”\__
A committee including representatives from the AAUP and from student and administrator groups formulates the _[Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students](https://www.aaup.org/report/joint-statement-rights-and-freedoms-students)_.
**1968**The AAUP publishes the first edition of _Policy Documents and Reports_, better known as the Redbook.
The AAUP issues [_The Role of the Faculty in the Accrediting of Colleges and Universities_](https://www.aaup.org/report/role-faculty-accrediting-colleges-and-universities).
**1969**AAUP membership peaks at around ninety thousand.
_The number of US military personnel in Vietnam peaks at more than 543,000._
**1970**The Council adopts a set of interpretive comments appended to the 1940 [_Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure_](https://www.aaup.org/report/1940-statement-principles-academic-freedom-and-tenure). Known as the 1970 Interpretive Comments, these footnotes are the result of joint meetings of the AAUP and the Association of American Colleges and reflect the experience gained over thirty years of applying the principles set forth in the 1940 _Statement_.
![Image 15](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/annualmtg(1).jpg)  
1970 annual meeting
_National Guard troops kill four students during a massive antiwar protest at Kent State University._
The faculties at Rutgers, St. John’s, and Oakland Universities become the first at four-year institutions to be represented in collective bargaining by the AAUP.
Committee W on the Status of Women in the Academic Profession is reactivated after an extended period of dormancy.
![Image 16](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/rossi1.jpg)  
Alice S. Rossi, chair of the reactivated Committee W
**1971**After much internal debate, the Council votes to “pursue collective bargaining . . . as a major additional way of realizing the Association’s goals in higher education” and to “allocate such resources and staff as are necessary for a vigorous selective development of this activity beyond present levels.”
The Special Committee on Nontenured Faculty is established “in recognition of the increasing numbers of faculty and Association members who are nontenured and in further recognition of the need to give special consideration to their status and rights.”
![Image 17](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/URI%20count.jpg)  
Votes are tallied in the 1971 collective bargaining election at  
 the University of Rhode Island. The AAUP defeated the National  
 Education Association in the election, and the University of Rhode  
 Island became the second state university on the East Coast to  
 be represented by the AAUP in bargaining.
**1972**_Title IX becomes law, barring discrimination based on sex at educational institutions that receive federal aid._
**1973**_US military involvement in the Vietnam War ends._
The AAUP’s collective bargaining chapters establish the Collective Bargaining Caucus, the predecessor to the Collective Bargaining Congress.
![Image 18](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/nlrb(1).jpg)  
National office staff members Jordan E. Kurland, Woodley B. Osborne, Matthew W. Finkin, and Charles L. Haslam (from left to right) after a National Labor Relations Board hearing
The annual meeting adopts the first _Statement on Collective Bargaining_.
Committee L on Predominantly Black Institutions is established “to develop ways and means of making the national AAUP more responsive to the needs of these institutions and their constituents.” The committee will later evolve into the current Committee on Historically Black Institutions and Scholars of Color.
![Image 19](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/commL1977a(1).jpg)  
A Committee L meeting
**1975**The Collective Bargaining Congress is formed.
The AAUP begins to disaggregate salary data by sex in its annual _Report on the Economic Status of the Profession_, providing concrete information about salary discrimination.
The Association issues the [_Statement on Teaching Evaluation_](https://www.aaup.org/report/statement-teaching-evaluation).
**1978**Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure approves the subcommittee report _On Full-Time Non-tenure-track Appointments_, the first major AAUP policy document to examine the problems associated with contingent faculty appointments. The report concludes that the use of such appointments is “inequitable, harmful to morale, and a threat to academic freedom.”
**1979**The _Bulletin of the AAUP_ merges with the _Academe_ newsletter and changes its name to _Academe: Bulletin of the AAUP_.
The first AAUP Collective Bargaining Institute—the predecessor to the Summer Institute—is held at Eastern Michigan University.
**1980**_In its ruling in_ NLRB v. Yeshiva _, the Supreme Court labels most tenured and tenure-track faculty members at private institutions “managerial” employees, thus denying them a protected right to bargain collectively. Justice William Brennan dissents, writing, “The notion that a faculty member’s professional competence could depend on his undivided loyalty to management is antithetical to the whole concept of academic freedom.”_
![Image 20](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/office.jpg)  
Ernst Benjamin, the AAUP’s general secretary from 1984 to 1994, at the Association’s former office on Fourteenth Street NW in Washington, DC
**1988**The AAUP issues the [_Statement on Academic Government for Institutions Engaged in Collective Bargaining_](https://www.aaup.org/report/statement-academic-government-institutions-engaged-collective-bargaining), which holds that “collective bargaining should not replace, but rather should ensure, effective traditional forms of shared governance.”
**1989**_The for-profit University of Phoenix establishes its “online campus,” the first to offer bachelor’s and master’s degrees._
**1990**The Council approves the creation of a standing Committee on Part-Time and Term-Appointed Faculty (now the Committee on Contingency and the Profession).
A meeting of the AAUP and other organizations at Wolf Trap produces the _[Statement on Academic Freedom and Artistic Expression](https://www.aaup.org/report/academic-freedom-and-artistic-expression)_.
**1991**The AAUP establishes a procedure for sanctioning institutions “for substantial noncompliance with standards of academic governance.”
**1994**_Mandatory retirement for tenured faculty is eliminated._
Lindenwood College becomes the first institution to be placed on the sanction list following an investigation into the administration’s dismantling of faculty governance structures.
![Image 21](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/Bennington2(1).jpg)  
A teach-in at Bennington College
**2001**The AAUP issues the [_Statement of Principles on Family Responsibilities and Academic Work_](https://www.aaup.org/report/statement-principles-family-responsibilities-and-academic-work), significantly updating an earlier statement on provisions for child-rearing.
_On September 11, terrorists crash hijacked airplanes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The US government responds to the attacks by passing the Patriot Act, creating the Department of Homeland Security, and launching wars in Afghanistan and Iraq._
![Image 22](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/CEW2001p(1).jpg)  
A Campus Equity Week Rally in Trenton, NJ
**2003**_The Supreme Court, in its decisions in_ Grutter v. Bollinger _and_ Gratz v. Bollinger _, upholds the use of affirmative action in college and university admissions, citing the educational benefits of diversity_.
The AAUP’s Special Committee on Academic Freedom and National Security in a Time of Crisis issues its [report](https://www.aaup.org/report/academic-freedom-and-national-security-time-crisis) on the risks to academic freedom and free inquiry posed by the response to the September 11 attacks.
![Image 23](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/Sanders(1).jpg)  
Jane Buck, then president of the AAUP, congratulates US Representative Bernie Sanders, who received the Henry T. Yost Award in 2004 for his leadership on higher education issues.
**2005**The Collective Bargaining Congress adopts and the Council endorses [_Academic Unionism_](http://www.aaupcbc.org/academic-unionism "(opens in a new window)"), a statement that delineates the principles underlying the AAUP’s approach to collective bargaining for faculty members and academic professionals.
**2006**_In a ruling with potential negative implications for academic freedom, the US Supreme Court in_ Garcetti v. Ceballos _restricts speech by public employees on matters related to their “official duties.”_
**2007**The report [_Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans Universities_](https://www.aaup.org/report/report-aaup-special-committee-hurricane-katrina-and-new-orleans-universities), written by a special nine-member investigating committee, examines violations of AAUP standards at five New Orleans institutions in the aftermath of the 2005 storm. Four administrations are censured, but ameliorative actions taken by the institutions in the following years lead to the lifting of the censures.
_The bursting of the bubble in the US housing market triggers a financial crisis and an extended economic downturn. Disinvestment in public higher education accelerates as the Great Recession ushers in new austerity measures._
**2009**A subcommittee of Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure [responds to the issues raised by the Supreme Court’s _Garcetti_ ruling](https://www.aaup.org/report/protecting-independent-faculty-voice-academic-freedom-after-garcetti-v-ceballos), arguing forcefully for the importance of protecting an independent faculty voice.
![Image 24](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/IMG_6354(1).jpg)  
Students and faculty at a rally supporting Oakland University professors (courtesy _Oakland Post_)
**2010**The AAUP publishes the first volume of its annual [_Journal of Academic Freedom_](https://www.aaup.org/reports-publications/journal-academic-freedom).
**2011**_A new law passed in Wisconsin denies many public employees, including faculty members at state colleges and universities, most collective bargaining rights. A similar measure passes in Ohio but is later repealed in a veto referendum._
The AAUP introduces [_Academe Blog_](http://academeblog.org/ "(opens in a new window)").
**2013**On January 1,the [AAUP Foundation](http://www.aaupfoundation.org/ "(opens in a new window)"), a charitable organization, is created as part of an organizational restructuring.*
![Image 25](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/si2013(1).jpg)  
A workshop at the AAUP Summer Institute
**2014**The AAUP’s book-length report [_Recommended Principles to Guide Academy-Industry Relationships_](https://www.aaup.org/report/recommended-principles-guide-academy-industry-relationships) is published.
The AAUP launches the [One Faculty campaign](https://www.aaup.org/get-involved/issue-campaigns/one-faculty) to unite the faculty around concrete improvements in working conditions, shared governance, economic security, and academic freedom for faculty members serving on contingent appointments.
The AAUP invites faculty members and others who care about the public mission of America’s colleges and universities to sign its centennial declaration, a document that enumerates ten core principles of higher education that are under threat.
Thirty-one academic, scholarly, and educational organizations endorse the 1940 [_Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure_](https://www.aaup.org/report/1940-statement-principles-academic-freedom-and-tenure), bringing the total number of [endorsers](https://www.aaup.org/endorsers-1940-statement) to 248 as the AAUP enters its centennial year.
**2015**Johns Hopkins University Press publishes the [eleventh edition of the AAUP’s Redbook](https://jhupbooks.press.jhu.edu/content/policy-documents-and-reports "(opens in a new window)") to coincide with the centennial.
![Image 26](https://www.aaup.org/sites/default/files/images/Redbook%20cover%20image.jpg)  
The centennial edition of the Redbook
* _Addendum_: In June 2019, both the AAUP annual meeting and the AAUP-CBC regular meeting voted overwhelmingly to approve a proposed package of [organizational changes](https://www.aaup.org/restructuring-information) that combined the AAUP-CBC and the AAUP. As of January 1, 2020, the AAUP-CBC was folded into the AAUP and former programs of the CBC became programs of the AAUP.
